record.paper_title: Open Problems in Partial Differential Equations Arising from Fluid Dynamics
record.original_question: For multidimensional compressible Euler equations with generic smooth initial data, smooth solutions can blow up in finite time. Can one characterize the structure of the singularities that form from such smooth data, and in particular determine when genuine shock formation occurs before the development of shell singularities?

evidence.quote: Structures of singularities and formation of shocks. ... However, the nature of singularities in the solutions is not clear except for special cases for which the singularities are shown to be shocks ... It is important to characterize the structures of singularities forming from smooth solutions in terms of initial data. In particular, it is of great interest to determine when shocks form first before the development of shell singularities.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the compressible Euler equations in $d\ge 2$ space dimensions for an ideal fluid:
$$\partial_t \rho + \nabla\cdot(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_t(\rho u)+\nabla\cdot(\rho u\otimes u)+\nabla p=0,\qquad \partial_t E+\nabla\cdot((E+p)u)=0,$$
where $\rho>0$ denotes density, $u\in\mathbb{R}^d$ velocity, $p$ pressure, and $E=\tfrac12\rho|u|^2+\rho e$ total energy, closed by an equation of state (e.g.\ ideal-gas $p=(\gamma-1)\rho e$, $\gamma>1$). It is known that for generic smooth (e.g.\ $C^\infty$, compactly supported perturbations of a constant state) initial data, the local-in-time smooth solution must lose regularity in finite time.

Provide a characterization, in terms of the initial data, of the structure of the singularities that first form from such smooth solutions. In particular:

(a) Classify the possible types of first singularities (e.g.\ genuine shocks formed by gradient catastrophe of an outgoing simple wave, versus "shell singularities" associated with focusing/collapse of characteristic surfaces of the acoustic metric, and any other admissible types).

(b) Give explicit, verifiable conditions on the initial data $(\rho_0,u_0,e_0)$ that determine which type of singularity occurs first, and in particular identify the open set (or generic class) of smooth initial data for which a genuine shock (a pre-shock with the canonical $C^{1/3}$ cusp followed by a discontinuity) forms strictly before any shell singularity develops.
artifact.status_search_result: Substantial recent progress has been made: Buckmaster–Shkoller–Vicol and Abbrescia–Speck, among others, have proven shock formation results for 2D and 3D compressible Euler (including with vorticity and entropy), and the geometry of maximal development and shell-type boundary structure has been described in multiple dimensions (e.g., Shkoller–Vicol, Inventiones 2024). However, a complete classification of singularity types from generic smooth multidimensional data, and sharp initial-data criteria distinguishing genuine shock formation from shell singularities, remains incomplete in full generality.

status_evidence.title: The geometry of maximal development and shock formation for the Euler equations in multiple space dimensions
status_evidence.snippet: Constructs a fundamental piece of the boundary of the maximal globally hyperbolic development for multi-dimensional compressible Euler, addressing the local shock development problem.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work characterizes maximal development and shell-type boundary structure for multi-D Euler, but only partially.

status_evidence.title: Formation and development of singularities for the compressible Euler equations
status_evidence.snippet: Complete description of formation and development of singularities for 2D compressible Euler under azimuthal symmetry, including C^{1/3} pre-shock and weak discontinuities.
status_evidence.claim: Full singularity classification is established under symmetry assumptions, leaving the general generic-data problem open.

status_evidence.title: Formation of point shocks for 3D compressible Euler
status_evidence.snippet: Detailed analysis of the self-steepening mechanism leading to the first point shock for 3D isentropic Euler with vorticity.
status_evidence.claim: Shock formation is proven for specific 3D regimes, but generic-data classification remains open.
